=== README.md (md) === # Advanced Sports Data Tutorials The companion refresher tutorials for the University of Nebraska-Lincoln's SPMC 460: Advanced Sports Data Analysis === inst/tutorials/01-aggregates/01-aggregates.Rmd (rmd) === --- title: "Advanced Sports Data Lesson 1: Aggregates review" output: learnr::tutorial: progressive: true allow_skip: true runtime: shiny_prerendered description: > Learn how to take lots of little things and total them up into bigger things. --- ```{r setup, include=FALSE} library(learnr) library(gradethis) library(tidyverse) library(glue) knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE) tutorial_options(exercise.completion=FALSE) ``` # Review ## The basics Students taking SPMC 460 should already be familiar with the basics of data analysis with the Tidyverse. Should. The problem with many of these students is they have the memories of squirrels on meth. Five minutes after they finish a class -- whoosh. It's right out of their heads. So we begin with some basics to jog the memory. The first reminder is that all notebooks start with library imports. Just about every assignment in this class will use, at a minimum, `library(tidyverse)` and `library(tidymodels)`. We'll get to tidymodels later. For now, run this. ```{r load-tidyverse, exercise=TRUE} library(tidyverse) ``` ```{r load-tidyverse-solution} library(tidyverse) ``` ```{r load-tidyverse-check} grade_this_code() ``` **From now on, if that's not the first line of your notebook, you're probably doing it wrong.** ## Loading data The next thing we need to do is to get some data to work with. We do that by reading it in. In our case, we're going to read data from a csv file -- a comma-separated values file. The CSV file we're going to read is every NBA player since the 1979-1980 season -- Larry Bird and Magic Johnson's rookie season. You can download the data here if you want to use it in your own notebook. **For purposes of this exercise, you don't need to do this. The data is included here if you want to try this in your own notebook.** ```{r echo=FALSE, class.output="bg-info", results="asis", message=FALSE, warning=FALSE} library(downloadthis) library(glue) dllink <- download_link( link = "http://mattwaite.github.io/sportsdatafiles/allplayers.csv", button_label = "Download csv file", button_type = "danger", has_icon = TRUE, icon = "fa fa-save", self_contained = FALSE ) glue("
For this walkthrough:
{dllink}
") ``` A reminder of what you are going to do. First, you are going to give your data a name -- let's use `players`. Then, you'll use the arrow -- `<-` to assign the results of what comes next to the name `players`. What comes next? We'll use the `read_csv` function to ... read a csv file. What goes inside the () after `read_csv`? The file name and location. To make our lives simpler here, we'll use the URL and read it directly from my website. ```{r load-data, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE} players <- read_csv("http://mattwaite.github.io/sportsdatafiles/allplayers.csv") nplayers <- nrow(players) avgminutes <- players |> group_by(Age) |> summarise( count = n(), mean_minutes = mean(MP), median_minutes = median(MP) ) |> arrange(desc(mean_minutes)) |> slice(1) threesleader <- players |> arrange(desc(`3P`)) |> slice(1) ``` ```{r load-data-exercise, exercise = TRUE} players <- read_csv("http://mattwaite.github.io/sportsdatafiles/allplayers.csv") ``` ```{r load-data-exercise-solution} players <- read_csv("http://mattwaite.github.io/sportsdatafiles/allplayers.csv") ``` ```{r load-data-exercise-check} grade_this_code() ``` ### Exercise 1: Using head to see your data
